Exercises Exercise 10.1 First headless runs Run three claude -p commands on one of your projects: one asking about the code, one piping a file in, and one with --output-format json . Look at the structure of the returned JSON. What to look for in the JSON Fields like result (the answer), the run's cost and the number of turns. In real automation it pays to monitor the cost field — that's how you keep a budget and spot runs that went wild. Exercise 10.2 A maintenance script Write a script (you can ask Claude to write it!) that runs with claude -p and performs a real maintenance task in your project: lint fixes, updating the README from the code, or adding JSDoc to public functions. Insist on a minimal --allowedTools and a --max-turns . Checkpoint Commit before the run; afterwards — git diff to review. If the script stops on a missing permission, add exactly the blocked tool to allowedTools — not everything. That's how you build least-privilege automation, iteratively. Exercise 10.3 @claude on a real repo Required: a GitHub account and a repo of your own ( setup guide if you don't have one yet). In your repo, run /install-github-app and complete the setup. Open an issue describing a small, precise feature, and tag: @claude implement this and open a PR . Review the resulting PR — critically, as if a new team member wrote it. What should happen Within minutes you'll see Claude respond on the issue with a progress checklist, and at the end — a link to a ready PR. If the result isn't perfect, continue the dialogue in the PR's comments: @claude the button should work on mobile too . That's a full handoff to asynchronous work. Self-check 1. What does the -p flag do? A one-shot run: question in, answer out, program exits Privacy mode Print

title: Lesson 11 · Fully autonomous agents — the Agent SDK
text: Lesson 11 of 13 Fully autonomous agents — the Agent SDK and working principles In this lesson we build our own agent in code with the Claude Agent SDK — the same engine that powers Claude Code itself — and learn the five principles that separate an autonomous agent that creates value from one that creates chaos. What you'll learn What the Claude Agent SDK is and why it's the best starting point A first agent in TypeScript and Python Adding custom tools and programmatic permissions The five principles of safe autonomy Where to go next What is the Agent SDK The Claude Agent SDK is a library (TypeScript and Python) that gives you, in code, everything that drives Claude Code: the agentic loop (think → tool → result → think...), the file and terminal tools, the permission system, subagents, hooks and MCP. Instead of building agent infrastructure from scratch — you get the proven infrastructure and assemble your agent on top: the logic, the boundaries, and the integration into your system. # TypeScript npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk # Python pip install claude-agent-sdk A first agent: 20 lines TypeScript agent.ts import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk"; const result = query({ prompt: "find all the TODOs in the project and summarize them into TODO_REPORT.md", options: { cwd: "/path/to/project", allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Write"], maxTurns: 20, }, }); for await (const message of result) { if (message.type === "assistant") { console.log(message.message.content); // watch the agent "think" } if (message.type === "result") { console.log("Summary:", message.result); console.log("Cost ($):", message.total_cost_usd); } } Python agent.py import anyio from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions async def main(): async for message in query( prompt="find all the TODOs in the project and summarize them into TODO_REPORT.md", options=ClaudeAgentOptions( cwd="/path/to/project", allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Write"], max_turns=20, ), ): print(message) anyio.run(main) Run it — and watch the agent work in the output: searching, reading, writing, returning a final result with a cost. This is a real autonomous agent : you gave a goal, and it chose the steps itself. A custom tool The real power: giving the agent tools from your world. Custom tools are defined as an in-process MCP server: tools.ts import { tool, createSdkMcpServer, query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk"; import { z } from "zod"; const sendAlert = tool( "send_alert", "Sends an alert to the ops team. Use only for high-severity incidents.", { message: z.string(), severity: z.enum(["low", "high"]) }, async (args) => { await notifyOps(args.message, args.severity); // your logic return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "Alert sent" }] }; } ); const opsServer = createSdkMcpServer({ name: "ops-tools", tools: [sendAlert], }); const result = query({ prompt: "check last night's logs. if there's a severe incident - send an alert", options: { mcpServers: { "ops-tools": opsServer }, allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep", "mcp__ops-tools__send_alert"], maxTurns: 30, }, }); Note the tool's description — "use only for severe incidents". As with Skills and subagents, the description is the interface between your intent and the agent's judgment. Want harder control? The SDK also supports hooks and canUseTool — your function approving or rejecting every tool call in real time, in code. The five principles of safe autonomy Everything you've learned in the course distills into five principles. An agent that satisfies all five — you can truly release: 1. A feedback loop the agent runs itself Autonomy without a way to verify success is guessing. Tests (Lesson 3), a browser (Lesson 7), compilation, lint — the agent needs a tool that tells it "you succeeded/failed" without a human. Phrase every task with a check criterion: "...and you're done only when all the tests are green" . 2. Boundaries in code, not promises Least-privilege permissions ( allowedTools ), blocking hooks (Lesson 6), readonly users (Lesson 7), deny rules and an isolated environment (Lessons 9–10). What's forbidden — make it impossible , not just "not recommended". 3. Quantitative brakes maxTurns per run, cost monitoring from the returned JSON, and an external timeout. An agent stuck in a loop should stop by itself — not when you notice the bill. 4. External memory and slice-based work Long tasks break into stages, each ending in a commit and a state-file update (PROGRESS.md — Lesson 4). An interrupted run resumes from the file, not from zero. Git is the backbone: every stage is reversible. 5. A human at the decision points "Fully" autonomous doesn't mean "without humans" — it means the human moves from the inner loop to the checkpoints: the agent works alone for hours, but the deliverable is a PR you approve, and alerts (Notification hooks, send_alert) summon you when something unusual happens. You manage; you don't chaperone. ✅ The final test Before releasing an agent to run alone, ask: "what's the worst that could happen in this run?" If the answer is "a messy git branch I'll delete" — go. If the answer includes a real database, money or customers — principle 2 is missing. Go back and strengthen boundaries. Exercises Exercise 11.1 Your first agent in code Run the TODO agent from the example (in whichever language suits you) on a real project. Then change the task to something of yours: generating a docs report, finding dead code, checking translation consistency. Follow the steps it chooses in the output. If something gets stuck Make sure the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable is set, and that allowedTools includes what the task truly requires (writing a report = needs Write). A "tool not allowed" error in the output is a precise hint at what's missing. Exercise 11.2 A custom tool + judgment Build a "project health checker" agent with one custom tool: report_status(status, details) that writes to a JSON file (or sends a real message — Telegram/Slack if you like). The task: "run tests and lint; report ok if all is well, and failed with details if not". Run it once on a healthy project and once on a broken one. What you're testing here That the agent uses your tool correctly : once with ok, once with failed + real failure details. If it reports ok on a broken project — sharpen the prompt ("actually run and read the output; don't assume"). Welcome to agent engineering. Exercise 11.3 Capstone: the nightly agent Put it all together: build an agent that runs on a schedule (cron or scheduled GitHub Actions) once a day on one of your repos, performing a maintenance task of your choice end to end — on a separate branch, with tests as the feedback loop, maxTurns, a state file, and a PR as the deliverable. Let it run three nights and review the results. Recommended frame Take nightly-deps.sh from Lesson 10 as the skeleton and swap the task: dead-code cleanup, improving test coverage ("add one test to the least-covered file"), or doc

title: Lesson 12 · Building an agent squad — principles, patterns, infrastructure
text: Lesson 12 of 13 Building an agent squad — principles, patterns and infrastructure In Lesson 8 you met subagents — helpers one agent activates. Now we level up: an agent squad — a group of agents with defined roles, divided work and a shared deliverable. Like the difference between one talented employee and a whole department working for you. What you'll learn When one agent stops being enough — and when a squad is a mistake The anatomy of a squad: roles, an orchestrator, shared memory and deliverable contracts Three organizational patterns: pipeline, orchestrator–workers, parallel Building it for real: in Claude Code and in the Agent SDK Why a squad at all? A single agent, however strong, has three structural limits: One context window. A truly large task (research + planning + execution + testing + docs) bloats the context until quality drops. You met this in Lesson 4. One hat at a time. Whoever wrote the code struggles to critique it objectively — true for humans, true for agents. A critic with separate instructions and a clean context finds problems the author misses. Serial execution. Five independent tasks with one agent run one after another. Five agents finish them in a fifth of the time. ⚠️ But don't get carried away A squad costs more (tokens), is harder to maintain, and harder to debug. The rule: always start with one agent, and split into a squad only when you actually hit one of the three limits above. A squad is a solution to a problem — not decoration. Anatomy of an agent squad Every successful squad, in any field, is built from the same four components: Component What it is How to implement Orchestrator Whoever breaks the goal into tasks, delegates and merges Claude Code's main conversation, or an SDK script Specialists An agent per role: its own instructions, tools, permissions Files in .claude/agents/ (Lesson 8) Shared memory Where the squad exchanges information and deliverables Files in the repo: SPEC.md , PROGRESS.md , an artifacts/ folder Deliverable contract A precise definition of what each role receives and returns An "input/output" section in each agent's system prompt 💡 The most important principle: deliverable contracts Agent squads almost always fail at the same point — agent A returns a vague deliverable, and agent B doesn't know what to do with it. The solution: every agent finishes with a defined deliverable — "a PLAN.md with a numbered step list", "a findings report in a table with a severity per row". A defined deliverable = a clean handoff. Three organizational patterns 1. Pipeline Agents work one after another , each receiving its predecessor's deliverable: planner → builder → checker → documenter. Simple, predictable, easy to debug — when something breaks, it's clear at which station. planner ──► builder ──► checker ──► documenter SPEC.md code report README Fits when work has a natural, fixed order and every stage depends on the previous one. 2. Orchestrator–Workers An orchestrating agent holds the big picture, breaks down the task, and delegates each part to a specialist — as needed, not necessarily in fixed order. The orchestrator decides in real time: "does the researcher's finding require another check? I'll send the checker again." ┌──► researcher orchestrator ┼──► builder (decides) └──► critic ▲______________│ (deliverables come back to it) Fits when the task requires judgment about "what now" — not a fixed script. 3. Parallel–Merge Split a task into independent parts, each agent works on one simultaneously , and a merge stage at the end. The clean way to do it in code: git worktrees — a separate working copy per agent, so they don't step on each other: macOS / Linux # a separate working copy per agent, each on its own branch git worktree add ../shop-payments feature/payments git worktree add ../shop-search feature/search # terminal 1: cd ../shop-payments && claude # terminal 2: cd ../shop-search && claude Windows (PowerShell) git worktree add ..\shop-payments feature/payments git worktree add ..\shop-search feature/search # a terminal window per agent: cd ..\shop-payments; claude cd ..\shop-search; claude Fits when parts are truly independent. The merge is where you pay the price — plan it in advance. Pattern When to choose it Weak point Pipeline A process with a clear, fixed order Slow — everything is serial Orchestrator–workers Dynamic judgment about work order is needed The orchestrator is a bottleneck and single point of failure Parallel Independent parts + a tight schedule Conflicts at the merge stage Building it, way 1: everything inside Claude Code The squad is defined as a set of files in .claude/agents/ (exactly like Lesson 8), and the main conversation serves as the orchestrator. The work script is packaged as a custom command — and the whole squad is launched with one word: .claude/commands/build-feature.md You are a squad orchestrator. Build the feature: $ARGUMENTS The working process, step by step: 1. Send planner to write SPEC.md with a detailed plan 2. Show me the plan and stop for approval 3. After approval - send coder to implement per the SPEC 4. Send test-writer to cover the new code with tests 5. Send code-reviewer for review; a critical finding goes back to coder 6. Summarize: what was built, what was tested, what remains open Note step 2: a stop for human approval at the decision point — principle 5 from Lesson 11, now at squad level. Building it, way 2: a squad in code with the Agent SDK In the SDK you define the team members inside the options, and the model delegates to them exactly like subagents: squad.ts import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk"; const result = query({ prompt: "build a complete 'Contact' page: planning, implementation, tests and review", options: { agents: { planner: { description: "Planner. Use first for any new feature.", prompt: "Write a short, numbered implementation plan to SPEC.md. Do not write code.", tools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Write"], }, coder: { description: "Implements according to an existing SPEC.md.", prompt: "Implement the SPEC.md steps one by one. Update PROGRESS.md after each step.", }, reviewer: { description: "Code reviewer. Use after every implementation.", prompt: "Review the diff. Return a findings table with severity. Do not edit files.", tools: ["Read", "Grep", "Bash"], }, }, maxTurns: 60, }, }); for await (const message of result) { if (message.type === "result") console.log(message.result); } Exactly the same principles: a role, a deliverable contract (SPEC.md, PROGRESS.md, a findings table), and permissions per need — the reviewer doesn't get Edit. Rules of thumb for a healthy squad 3–5 roles are usually enough. A squad of ten agents is almost always a sign the problem was decomposed wrong. One role = one responsibility. If an agent's description doesn't fit in a sentence, the role is too broad. At least one critic. A squad with no review role (reviewer, checker, editor) is an assembly line of fast mistakes. Everything through shared me

title: Lesson 13 · Agent squads across five industries
text: Lesson 13 of 13 · The summit Agent squads across five industries — real-world examples The patterns from Lesson 12 are a skeleton — now we put flesh on it. Five squads from five different worlds: development, content and marketing, data, operations, and customer service. For each: the roles, the chosen pattern and why, and downloadable agent files. What you'll learn How to translate a problem from any field into a squad design Five detailed squads, from five industries The principles that repeat in all of them — regardless of field The capstone: a squad for your own world ⬇️ Every agent — downloadable Every agent in this lesson's tables is a link to a ready agent file: save it into .claude/agents/ in your project and it's live. You can also grab all 100 agents in one zip . Note: the agent files are currently written in Hebrew — asking Claude to translate one to English is a ten-second task (and good practice). 1. The development world: "the feature squad" 🛠️ The problem: a medium-to-large feature demands planning, implementation, tests and review — and with a single agent that ends in bloated context and declining quality. The pattern: a pipeline with a stop for human approval after planning (exactly what we built in Lesson 12). Role Tools Deliverable (the contract) planner — planner read & search only + Write for the SPEC SPEC.md : numbered steps + success criterion coder — implementer full code + PROGRESS.md update after every step test-writer — tester full passing tests for the new code code-reviewer — reviewer read only + git diff a graded findings table The lesson from this world: the critic must be separate from the implementer — and without write permissions, so the review stays a review. Scaling up: the full engineering organization The feature squad is the core, but a whole engineering org runs more teams alongside it: Team The agents and their roles Security team Reviews every change and dependency before production threat-modeler — analyzes risks for every new feature at the SPEC stage secrets-scanner — scans for secrets and keys in code and git history dependency-auditor — checks known vulnerabilities in dependencies and prioritizes fixes authz-reviewer — checks permissions and access on every new endpoint security-reporter — merges the findings into one graded report Infrastructure (DevOps) The road from code to servers — fast, cheap, reversible iac-writer — writes and updates infrastructure-as-code (Terraform, K8s) ci-doctor — diagnoses CI failures and fixes or reports cost-watcher — monitors cloud costs and flags anomalies capacity-planner — plans resources from load trends rollback-guardian — ensures every change has a ready way back Quality (QA) A testing layer beyond the feature squad's own tests e2e-writer — end-to-end scenarios in a real browser (Lesson 7) perf-tester — measures performance and catches slow regressions a11y-checker — accessibility: contrast, keyboard, screen readers regression-hunter — turns every old bug into a test that prevents its return Maintenance & docs The quiet work that keeps the project healthy dep-updater — nightly dependency updates on a separate branch (Lesson 10) dead-code-cleaner — finds and removes code with no callers api-doc-writer — keeps the docs in sync with the code changelog-writer — writes the change list for every release How the teams meet: at the Pull Request. The feature squad produces, security and QA review every PR, infrastructure provides the road to production — and maintenance sweeps through everything else in the background. 2. Content and marketing: "the magazine desk" ✍️ The problem: a company blog post demands research, writing, editing and search optimization — four different skills a rushed single writer does averagely. The pattern: a pipeline, with the editor as a gatekeeper who may send a draft back. Role Tools Deliverable (the contract) researcher — researcher WebSearch, Read, Write research.md : facts + a source for every claim copywriter — writer Read, Write a draft from research.md only — no invented facts editor — editor Read, Edit an edited version + notes; may send back to the writer seo-checker — SEO checker Read, Write a report: titles, description, keywords, internal links The lesson from this world: the researcher's contract ("a source for every claim") is what keeps the whole squad from inventing facts. Credibility is built at the start of the chain. Scaling up: the full marketing department Team The agents and their roles Social team Distributes and adapts the content per platform trend-scout — spots rising topics in the field before everyone post-writer — converts each article into per-network versions engagement-analyst — analyzes what worked, what didn't, and why calendar-planner — builds a balanced weekly publishing calendar Campaigns team Paid advertising measured to the last dollar audience-profiler — defines target audiences and a message per audience ad-copywriter — writes ad variants tailored to each audience ab-test-designer — designs A/B experiments with clear success metrics budget-monitor — tracks cost-per-conversion and flags waste SEO team Expands the basic SEO check into strategy keyword-researcher — researches search phrases and competition levels content-gap-analyst — finds topics competitors cover and you don't internal-linker — suggests internal links between existing content rank-tracker — tracks rankings and reports changes Brand team Keeps all content sounding like one organization brand-guardian — enforces consistent tone, messaging and terminology visual-brief-writer — writes precise briefs for designers consistency-checker — scans site and materials for contradictions How the teams meet: the magazine produces, social and campaigns distribute, SEO steers the next topics — and the brand-guardian reviews everyone before publishing. 3. The data world: "the weekly report squad" 📊 The problem: every week the same business question ("what happened to sales and why") must be answered from raw data — a process of collection, cleaning, analysis and presentation. The pattern: orchestrator–workers. Why not a pipeline? Because the analysis dictates what follows: an anomaly demands another dive, a normal week does not. The orchestrator decides. Role Tools Deliverable (the contract) collector — collector a database MCP (readonly!) data/raw_week.csv + query documentation cleaner — cleaner Read, Write, Bash (python) data/clean_week.csv + a log: what was fixed and why analyst — analyst Read, Write, Bash (python) findings.md : 3–5 findings + a confidence level each visualizer — visualizer Read, Write charts + an HTML report page The lesson from this world: two things. One — readonly database permissions (Lesson 7) are what allow the squad to run unsupervised. Two — "a confidence level per finding" in the analyst's contract keeps the report from presenting a guess as a fact.
